newsitem.title: USA: Clinton ready for knee surgery.
newsitem.headline: Clinton ready for knee surgery.

text.p: President Bill Clinton entered Bethesda naval hospital on Friday for surgery to repair a knee tendon torn during a late-night stumble in Florida.

The knee-buckling tumble on the estate of golfer Greg Norman -- "he heard a very loud pop," one aide said -- will put Clinton on crutches for weeks, but he vowed it would not delay his summit with Russian President Boris Yeltsin in Finland next week and doctors said he may well be right.

That remained to be seen, however, and the episode had other diplomatic ripple effects as well, including questions as to whether Hillary Rodham Clinton would begin a two-week tour of six African nations right on schedule Saturday.

With Clinton reported cracking jokes and trying to keep his spirits up, doctors described the surgery as a relatively straightforward and common affair likely to last about an hour or so as surgeons drill holes into his kneecap to hold sutures to reattach his quadriceps tendon to the knee.
He was expected to spend the night in the hospital at the National Naval Medical Centre, which is the regular site of presidential medical treatment in this Washington suburb.

The president was facing weeks of walking on crutches and a long recovery, an unpleasant prospect for an active 50-year-old who loves to jog and was getting ready for a big weekend of golf when he tripped on a step and injured himself at Norman's Jupiter, Florida, estate.

Clinton made a dramatic arrival at Andrews Air Force Base after his Air Force One flight from Florida. A blue elevator truck raised a platform from the rain-slick tarmac to the front door of the plane. Secret Service agents helped him on board and he was lowered to the ground.

He emerged with a crutch under his right arm and his left arm around the shoulders of a Secret Service agent. Someone held a large black umbrella over his head as he hopped left-footed to a black recreation vehicle in a driving rain. Mrs. Clinton hovered nearby, overseeing his progress.
Doctors said he would be conscious under an anaesthetic that numbs from the midsection down during his surgery, avoiding any need for a temporary transfer of power to Vice President Al Gore.

Left unclear was whether Clinton would be able to followthrough on his pledge to attend the March 19-20 summit in Helsinki, Finland, with Yeltsin, who is himself recovering from heart surgery and pneumonia.
On his departure from West Palm Beach, Fla., Clinton insisted he would proceed, saying, "It will go on, you bet."
Orthopedic surgeons and sports medicine experts consulted by Reuters said they thought there was a very good chance he would feel well enough to go through with the trip.
"Certainly, the way he travels, I would think he would be able to go," said Dr. Stephen Haas, a Washington orthopedist who operated on Gore when the vice president ripped his Achilles tendon in 1994.
But the White House was more cautious. "We're going to wait and see how the surgery goes," said spokesman Mike McCurry.

A senior State Department official said one possible diplomatic casualty of the presidential mishap could be a scheduled Monday meeting with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, which might have to be scrapped.
The episode also seemed likely to delay slightly Mrs. Clinton's planned departure on Saturday on her African trip.
Her spokesman Neel Lattimore said the trip was still on but Mrs. Clinton wanted to wait and see the severity of her husband's injury before deciding when to leave.

Dr. Joel Cohen, an orthopedic surgeon at St. Mary's Hospital in West Palm Beach, Florida, where the president had X-rays, told reporters Clinton's leg would be immobilized in a brace and that he would be on crutches for several weeks.
Doctors said the injury was not uncommon and they described it as relatively minor.

"He has a tear in the quadriceps tendon," Cohen said. "It's not an uncommon injury. The expectation would be a return to full activity. They're going to sew the tendon back to his kneecap. He literally pulled the tendon from the bone."

Clinton's personal physician, U.S. Navy Captain Connie Mariano, said the president was in great pain after the fall, but had been given a non-narcotic anti-inflammatory painkiller and remained in good spirits.

Cohen said normally this kind of injury put the patient in a splint and on crutches for several weeks followed by a course of rehabilitation. He said full recovery could take between six weeks and three months.
